Moving from chatting back and forth with agents, to having agents that you spin up in the background to do useful work for you is probably on the order of 100X or 1000X more token consumption than what we’re seeing today. 

Most work right now is essentially rate limited by our ability to process and work with information. Moving data between systems. Reviewing a document. Looking through code for security issues. Processing log data to look for even patterns. Looking up information about a prospective client. Almost all of knowledge work is constrained by these steps, and AI has become a huge unlock to that. 

So our first step was to use AI to do these individual tasks much faster for us. That was the chatbot phenomenon that we have been experiencing for the past 3+ years. But we can still then only augment the work that we remain in the loop for, and we’re highly limited by our ability to parallelize this work by our own bandwidth and context.

But where we’re going is quite different. As AI models continue to improve at incredible rates, we can hand off more and more work to the agent. First it’s letting the agent run with a harder problem. Then it’s giving a few agents multiple parts of a task at once. But we’re not far off from being able to throw an arbitrary number of agents at a problem and just say “come back when you’ve accomplished this goal”. 

Now imagine that agent swarm for any problem we can think of. Protecting our codebases, data, and systems. QAing every change we make and make sure all our infrastructure is robust and does what it should. Looking through every document for potential risks. Auditing this company with vastly more data reviewed. And on and on. Most of this isn’t even replacing existing work we do, it’s all net new. 

These agents will get deployed as swarms by people, by workflows, by triggers, and by other agents. And none of this would be possible if the models weren’t getting better, and if the cost of AI didn’t make it affordable. Both of those trends though are playing out. Now the next frontier is just having enough compute. But this is where it’s heading.

They did it. They made a Muse open weights model, which is a huge step forward for OSS in the US. 

This is going to further accelerate AI diffusion because enterprises will be able to mix and match frontier performance for orchestration and high end tasks, while being able to have low cost and tailored post trained models for repeatable workflows. 

Overall this dramatically increases token consumption and workloads across the stack. Great to see Meta doing this.

Cyber is going to be one of the biggest spaces for AI agents in the future. 

Obviously the risks of software exploits and the attack surface area increases 100 fold due to the ability for agents to work through any crack to find what they’re looking for.

But this goes the other way as well. The ability to have agent swarms review every line of code, test any number of permutations of exploits, and research any incident faster than humans as they happen, will be a huge boost in how we secure systems in the future. 

Cyber has always been a category where it’s hard to keep up with (and triage) all the incoming risks, alerts, and changes in the enterprise and across all system. You can never hire enough people or work through the backlog of all known risks. Agents actually give you a chance finally to have far better coverage of this.

This is going to be a huge opportunity as well because we’ll see plays at the labs, data providers, the layer of the network and firewall, identity, devices and endpoints, SDLC, and even how we protect our data in the enterprise. Lots of interesting dimensions to cyber at the moment.

Results based on +5K real-world agentic sessions are in: Muse Wonder (Max) by @AIatMeta just landed in the Agent Arena at #12 with +6.4% net improvement.

This result is +2.8 pts and four places above Muse Spark 1.3 (Max) at #16 with +3.6%. The added performance of Muse Wonder (Max) comes at a higher price: $1.13 median cost per task vs. $0.54 for Spark 1.3, or about 2.1× the cost.

Compared with nearby models in Agent Arena, Muse Wonder (Max) shows cost efficiency: at $1.13/task, it comes within 1 percentage point of #10 GPT-5.6 Sol (xHigh) at 25% lower cost, and within 2pts of #9 Claude Fable 5 (High) at 67% lower cost.

By category, Muse Wonder (Max) does better in Chat, Work and Code vs. Muse Spark 1.3:
- Chat: #12 (+6.5%) vs. #15 (+3.3%) 
- Work: #13 (+6.8%) vs. #18 (+3.7%)
- Code: #15 (+5.2%) vs. #18 (+4.2%)

Congrats to the @AIatMeta team on this release!

Claude Haiku 5.5 (High) by @AnthropicAI has landed in the Agent Arena! Across +20.5K real-world agentic sessions from our global community of users, this release scored +1.48% net improvement and landed at #27 overall.

Its strongest Agent Arena category is Code, where it ranks #15 with +4.83% net improvement.

Haiku 5.5 shows cost efficiency with a median cost per task of $0.09, placing it just outside the Agent Arena Pareto frontier. Nearby on the Pareto frontier, GPT-6 Luna (Max) delivers +3.19% at $0.08/task.

Compared to GPT-5.4 (High) priced at $0.63/task in the #26 spot, Haiku 5.5 costs 86% less. Although Haiku 5.5's net improvement score is lower than other Anthropic models, this model is 97–99% cheaper per task than Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Max), Fable 5.1 (Max), and Opus 5.5 (Max).

Congrats again to the @AnthropicAI team on this release!

Welcome to the era of embodied AI.

We are launching AA-Robotics v0.1, our research preview that measures frontier language model performance on understanding, planning, and acting in the physical world. In v0.1, each model is given control of a 6-axis robot arm (5 joints and a gripper) and a simple objective. We’re releasing results for our first eight tasks today.

We find that frontier language models in coding agent harnesses have recently become capable of directly manipulating robot arms for simple tasks. Today, they are far too slow and expensive for any kind of production usage - nearly two orders of magnitude worse than human baselines. We expect this to change quickly.

GPT-6 Astra places first in AA-Robotics v0.1, followed by GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon and Claude Opus 5.5.

AA-Robotics v0.1 details:

➤ Our first eight tasks test a range of capabilities: control and dexterity (precise grasping and object handling), spatial reasoning (how objects interact with one another) and adaptability (how models respond to the unexpected)

➤ Models get only brief instructions: how to connect to the robot arm (via a simple HTTP API), the arm's name and how to submit an attempt. They can view the scene through four cameras and write and run code to plan and send movements

➤ Once a model submits an attempt, its end state is graded against the task's pass criteria. A pass scores 100; an incomplete attempt earns partial credit. All attempts are zero-shot

Key findings:

➤ The GPT family tops the leaderboard: GPT-6 Astra scores 69, ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol at 65 and Gemini 4 Argon at 55. Claude Opus 5.5 (49) and Claude Fable 5.1 (46) trail

➤ Today’s models are incredibly slow at our tasks, taking ~30 minutes on average to complete each tabletop task

➤ Cost varies widely: GPT-6.1 Sol is the cheapest at $1.93 per task on average; GPT-6 Astra, the most expensive, costs $16.36, more than eight times as much

➤ Compared with a human, today's best-performing frontier language models are ~100x slower and ~10x more expensive

More results, clips, and how AA-Robotics v0.1 works follow in the thread below.

We asked AI models to build the Eiffel Tower in 3D, offline. Two of them added all 72 scientists' names to it, in order, from memory

We did not expect this. Every AA-3D model got the same brief of about 200 words, on the tower's shape, lattice, platforms and lighting. It never mentions the names.

Gustave Eiffel put the names of 72 French scientists, engineers, and mathematicians under the tower's first platform, 18 on each side. Claude Opus 5.5 and Grok 4.7 wrote all 72, with each side in the real order.

Claude Opus 5.5 also put each set on the side that faces the same way in Paris.

Each model built its scene as an agent in a sandbox with no internet access. In both runs, the names first appear in code the model wrote, never in a file or tool output it read.

Congratulations to @spacexai, @elonmusk and @AnthropicAI on two seriously knowledgeable models

NVIDIA's RTX Spark N1X puts up to 128 GB of unified memory and a Blackwell GPU in a Windows laptop. In our first AA-AgentPerf-Local results, an RTX Spark laptop completes our local agent workload on Qwen3.8 27B in 18.7 minutes

RTX Spark's N1X chip is essentially the GB10 from DGX Spark (20-core Arm CPU, 6,144-core Blackwell GPU), with up to 128 GB of memory at 300 GB/s. We tested a prototype 15-inch Surface Laptop Ultra (128 GB, $5,900), plugged in with Windows set to high-performance mode, using NVIDIA's published llama.cpp recipes where available

Key results:

➤ On Qwen3.8 27B the RTX Spark laptop finishes our default workload (8 recorded agent tasks, 168 model turns) in 18.7 minutes, close to DGX Spark (17.3), 2.0x faster than the MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 64 GB, 37.6) and 1.8x faster than the AMD Ryzen AI Halo (34.5). The GeForce RTX 5090 desktop is fastest, at 4.9 minutes

➤ On Qwen3.6 35B A3B it takes 7.6 minutes, close to DGX Spark (7.3), and 1.6x faster than the MacBook Pro (11.9)

➤ On Ling 3.0 Flash, the largest current model we test, it takes 15.3 minutes, close to DGX Spark (14.9) and 1.6x faster than the Ryzen AI Halo (25.1). Its 77 GB of weights do not fit on the MacBook Pro or the RTX 5090

This is one of the most exhilarating times in technology, and this challenge was yet another jaw-dropping moment.

When the details of OpenAI’s agent escape and Hugging Face hack started to emerge, it became clear that agent containment would be one of the most important priorities for any AI infra company.

There are two classes of escapes: ① "escape the network" and ② “escape the matrix” 😁, as in, break the spell of virtualization. OpenAI was the former, where an agent not supposed to have internet access… gained it by hacking another system. Genuinely astonishing and worrisome.

Through this challenge, however, we discovered something even more groundbreaking. A talented white-hat researcher, armed with a swarm of AI agents, expertise and perseverance, "pierced through" the Linux virtualization boundary that nearly every cloud sandbox provider in the world banks on today.

I'm very thankful we got the report, were able to quickly move to protect our customers, found no evidence of customer data compromise, and collaborated with many industry partners to protect the wider internet.

Our confidence and conviction in Vercel Sandbox are even greater now, after some of the smartest, most motivated researchers in the world, and their agents, gave it their best shot.
I recently described the modern scalable agent architecture as: 🧠 brain, 🙌 hands, 🗃️ files. The files are here.

Vercel Daemons

Coined in MIT in 1963, "we fancifully began to use the word daemon to describe background processes that worked tirelessly to perform system chores", inspired by Maxwell’s thought experiment of an imaginary agent in thermodynamics.

You can pause frontier research today, and it would take AI another 10 years to diffuse into the economy. We're working with solutions partners to accelerate that.
